title: From surviving archive back into circulation: reverse bridges from the source registry to the UK microscopy corpus
method: Names and object systems newly prioritized in the source registry were searched back through the project's nineteenth-century UK microscopy corpus. Hits are retained only when the surrounding record changes what can be asked of the surviving collection; generic citations and homonyms are excluded.

bridges.archive_anchor: Whipple preserves Elcock's slides, raw/preparatory material, tools, mounting supplies, labels, books and ephemera.

corpus_events.source: Journal of the Postal Microscopical Society, vol. II
corpus_events.event: Elcock reports collecting abundant Foraminifera at Southport and gives practical instructions for scraping, washing, drying, floating and preparing the material.
corpus_events.research_use: Connects surviving workshop raw material and finished Foraminifera slides to a named field-collection and processing practice.

corpus_events.source: Journal of Microscopy and Natural Science, vol. III
corpus_events.event: The Society's annual review singles out six Elcock communications on Foraminifera and says they were especially valuable when studied in connection with the circulating slides.
corpus_events.research_use: Elcock's slides were not only commercial products; in the postal society they operated as travelling teaching/research objects coordinated with members' notes.

corpus_events.source: Journal of Microscopy and Natural Science, vol. III
corpus_events.event: The report observes that a slide circulating without information could suddenly become valuable when a member supplied careful notes, immediately after discussion of Elcock/Malcomson Foraminifera work.
corpus_events.research_use: Provides an explicit contemporary statement that interpretive documentation could change the epistemic value of an otherwise familiar circulating slide.

corpus_events.source: Journal of Microscopy and Natural Science, vol. III
corpus_events.event: Annual classified list records six Elcock Foraminifera subjects, including Atlantic dredgings, isomorphism and named genera/species.
corpus_events.research_use: Supplies subject-level targets for matching surviving Elcock preparations and labels.

corpus_events.source: Journal of Microscopy and Natural Science, vol. III
corpus_events.event: Classified technical list includes Elcock, 'On Gum for Mounting Foraminifera.'
corpus_events.research_use: Direct bridge from workshop material/mounting media to a named method communication.

corpus_events.source: Journal of Microscopy and Natural Science, vol. IV
corpus_events.event: Advertisements offer Elcock Foraminifera 'Type Slides' Nos. 1 and 2, each with fifty named species visible in the field, priced at twenty shillings each; other slides and student/lecture series were in preparation. Retail routes include Beck & Beck, Watson & Sons, Charles Collins, E. Ward and Alfred Allen.
corpus_events.research_use: Turns the Whipple archive into a complete chain candidate: field collection → preparation method → society circulation/notes → standardized multi-species Type Slide → price → retailer network → surviving workshop archive.

next_extraction: search Whipple labels for Type Slide No. 1 / No. 2
identify any fifty-species arrangements
transcribe retailer/printed ephemera
match Southport/Antrim/Lias/London Clay material to surviving packets or slides
look for gum/media containers associated with Foraminifera

bridges.actor_or_collection: Charles Sedgwick Minot / Harvard Embryological Collection
bridges.archive_anchor: Harvard preserves serial embryo sections, original cards and drawings; Minot papers survive at Countway.

corpus_events.event: British journal notice reports Minot's new microtome for cutting a series of sections, recently described to the Boston Society of Natural History.
corpus_events.research_use: Establishes British contemporary awareness of Minot's serial-section apparatus before the later Harvard Embryological Collection matured.

corpus_events.source: Monthly Microscopical Journal, vol. XVIII, 'Histology and Embryology'
corpus_events.event: Minot explains why tissues require special treatment, discusses hand/machine section cutting, hardening, paraffin, staining and mounting, and ends with practical advice on simple research microscopes and objectives.
corpus_events.research_use: The surviving Harvard serial-section archive can be read against Minot's own contemporary technical programme rather than only later collection descriptions.

next_extraction: identify which techniques in 1877 recur in early HEC object records
date-filter HEC records to nineteenth century
crosswalk stains/section thickness/preparator fields to Minot publications and correspondence

bridges.actor_or_collection: Henri Van Heurck distributed scientific estate
bridges.archive_anchor: Van Heurck's diatoms, books and microscopy instruments later became institutionally distributed across Belgian repositories.

corpus_events.source: Journal of the Royal Microscopical Society
corpus_events.event: Bibliographic notice reports a new edition of Van Heurck's microscopy/botany work in preparation and describes his diatom collection as one of the most important then existing, with no fewer than 10,000 specimens and major type/original material.
corpus_events.research_use: Provides a dated contemporary state of the collection before the later estate-level dispersal; the '10,000' figure must remain a historical claim, not a current object count.

corpus_events.source: Journal of the Royal Microscopical Society
corpus_events.event: A report on Van Heurck's diatom work emphasizes drawings made from authentic specimens/types in his botanical museum, with Grunow involved in drawing plates and high-power objectives used for difficult forms.
corpus_events.research_use: Shows the collection operating as an authentication infrastructure connecting type material, drawing, microscopy and publication before later institutional dispersal.

corpus_events.source: Journal of the Royal Microscopical Society
corpus_events.event: Van Heurck sends mounted Amphipleura pellucida preparations and mounting-medium experiments into RMS meeting/exhibition contexts.
corpus_events.research_use: Adds object circulation and mounting technique to the later estate history.

next_extraction: capture dated historical counts separately
identify surviving authentic/type slides in Meise
trace Grunow-linked material and annotations
separate botanical/diatom material transfer from instrument/library transfers

bridges.actor_or_collection: John Thomas Norman / St Andrews surviving slides
bridges.archive_anchor: St Andrews preserves Norman-labelled slides and explicitly links them to his 1872 catalogue of 2,584 offerings.

corpus_events.event: Exchange column offers 'Norman's prepared microscopical slides and others' in return for fossils.
corpus_events.research_use: Shows Norman objects entering secondary exchange immediately in the catalogue period; maker identity remained useful enough to advertise the slides by name.

corpus_events.event: A microscopist tests a foreign objective on named preparations including Nitzschia sigmoidea mounted dry by Norman and Navicula rhomboides dry by Norman, alongside Topping slides.
corpus_events.research_use: A commercial slide becomes a test/comparison object for judging optical performance, demonstrating epistemic reuse after purchase.

next_extraction: transcribe St Andrews Norman slide subjects
match to 1872 catalogue
search corpus for the same subjects + Norman
record secondary retailer labels and current sleeve coordinates

bridges.archive_anchor: Whipple preserves an 1840–1870 cabinet containing Pritchard-labelled commercial slides, homemade preparations, broken slides and slide papers.

corpus_events.event: Historical notice says Pritchard claimed introduction of Canada balsam for mounting and cites his 1837 catalogue, which lists balsam-mounted objects and prices: transparent-object cases, opaque-object cases, selected sets by the dozen, and fossil-wood sections.
corpus_events.research_use: Provides a printed price/format system directly relevant to the catalogue-derived labels physically surviving in the Whipple cabinet.

next_extraction: photograph Pritchard catalogue-derived labels
identify whether cabinet objects fit the 1837 transparent/opaque/set categories
compare physical case/tray architecture with advertised sets
retain broken and homemade material as evidence of later cabinet use

general_result: The source registry is already feeding the corpus back into object research. Elcock is the clearest gain: a newly prioritized surviving workshop archive can now be connected to named collection sites, preparation technique, postal-society slide circulation, interpretive note-making, standardized Type Slides, prices and a multi-city retailer network. This is stronger than treating the archive as a static maker collection.
guard: These bridges connect actors, practices, series and institutional contexts. Unless a label, number, catalogue row or other object-specific evidence closes the identity, they do not prove that a particular surviving slide is the same physical object described in the corpus event.
